newsitem.title: HAITI: Haitian anger grows over exiled coup leaders.
newsitem.headline: Haitian anger grows over exiled coup leaders.

text.p: Two years ago they were among the world's pariahs, leaders of a bloody military coup that prompted President Bill Clinton to send thousands of U.S. troops to occupy Haiti and oust them from power.

But two years after the international force restored then President Jean-Bertrand Aristide on Oct. 15, 1994, the men who ousted Haiti's first freely-elected president and ruled the Caribbean nation during a brutal three-year dictatorship were living in comfortable exile.

Crowds of Haitians demonstrated in the capital city on Sept. 30, the fifth anniversary of the coup, calling for retribution against those responsible. The nation -- the western hemisphere's poorest -- fights rampant unemployment and illiteracy while rebuilding its justice system.
"They killed, stole, raped children and adults, emptied state coffers and spread insecurity in the four corners of the country," one speaker shouted to the crowd during the protest.
Coup victims have reported abuses to international organisations, such as the Organisation of American States, and have said they are angry at a lack of reparations.

"I believe justice will be done because I know the Haitian people are watching," Aristide, who left office in February after the election of President Rene Preval, told Reuters in a recent interview. "And if it is not done, they (the people) will move to speed up the process."

Lieut. Gen. Raoul Cedras, the lantern-jawed soldier who was the most visible coup leader, left Haiti on a U.S. military aircraft for Panama two years ago on Sunday with his family and fellow coup leader Brigadier Gen. Philippe Biamby.

Today, Cedras, his wife, nanny and three children live in Panama City's exclusive Punta Paitilla district. Their home is an undistinguished tower block called the Winston Churchill, where Cedras has told friends he is writing his memoirs.
Biamby, who had been Haiti's Army Chief of Staff, still lives with the Cedras family, but neither he nor his mentor is said to be short on cash.

In exchange for their agreement to leave Haiti peacefully, the U.S. government agreed to grant Cedras and Biamby access to their money, which had been frozen in U.S. bank accounts. Citing U.S. Treasury Department officials, the New York Times estimated those accounts held some $79 million.

The U.S. government agreed to lease Cedras' three homes in Haiti, two in the capital and a third on the beach, for between $5,000 and $12,000 a month, paying at least six months rent to Cedras in advance upon his departure.
No one is sure where Cedras and Biamby got their money, although many analysts here said they stole it from Haiti's state coffers, possibly including army pension funds.

Soldiers who served under Cedras have been demonstrating in Port-au-Prince and have allegedly carried out terrorist activities, including an August attack on a police station in the capital, because they have not received their pensions.

The third coup leader, the feared ex-colonel and Port-au-Prince Police Chief Michel Francois, left Haiti on Oct. 4 for the Dominican Republic, the home of his brother, where he had extensive business holdings.

Francois and ex-Col. Franck Romain, a member of the Haitian military also considered responsible for human rights abuses, were arrested by Dominican authorities in April 1996 and deported to Honduras after Preval visited Santo Domingo.
Francois also was alleged have made off with millions, allegedly gained through running contraband and drugs.
According to Honduran Interior Minister Efrain Moncada, the two men gave up their rights to participate in foreign or domestic politics in exchange for asylum.

The three Haitian coup leaders continued a long line of Haitian strongmen sent into exile without answering for their crimes. Perhaps the best known of those exiles was Jean-Claude "Baby Doc" Duvalier, who fled Haiti in 1986 and now lives outside Paris, although perhaps less comfortably than the leaders of the 1991 coup.
His wife, who divorced him in 1991, is said to have spent most of his fortune.
